newsitem.title: USA: US May NAPM index jump shows manufacturing strong.
newsitem.headline: US May NAPM index jump shows manufacturing strong.

text.p: A jump in the May National Association of Purchasing Management's (NAPM) index which showed the manufacturing sector of the economy rebounded in May could indicate that production will strengthen over the summer, economists said.
The National Association of Purchasing Management said its index jumped to 57.1 in May from a more tempered reading of 54.2 in April.
A reading above 50 on a NAPM index points to an expanding economy. A reading below 50 points to a contracting economy.
On the price front, the news was good for the inflation-fearful credit markets.
The NAPM inflation index read 48.4 in May, down from 49.6 in April.
But promising future strength for the manufacturing sector, the NAPM said its new orders index rose to 64.2 in May, the highest level since July of 1994, from 57.9 in April.

"The NAPM index shows that the economy is still healthy but that there are not a lot of price pressures, which is an encouraging development," said Gary Thayer, chief economist at A.G. Edwards & Sons Inc.

Thayer said "probably the most important component of the NAPM index is the new orders index which is up sharply, perhaps suggesting that the slowdown that we saw in the first couple of months in the second quarter of the year might be temporary."
Thayer said the production index reading at 57.0 versus 56.6 in April was still moderate.
"But the new orders component was up strongly which suggests that over the summer, we could see faster, or stronger, production," he said.
The NAPM said its employment index changed little in May, easing to 52.6 from 52.8 in April.
The NAPM jump to 57.1 exceeded economists' forecasts. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast that the NAPM index would read 53.9 in May, off from 54.2 in April.
The bond market weakened immediately after the jump in the overall NAPM index was reported.
Just before the release, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was up 6/32 to 96-20/32, yielding 6.89 percent.
Ten minutes after the report, the 30-year Treasury bond was down 6/32 to 96-8/32, its yield up to 6.92 percent.
David Jones, chief economist at Aubrey G. Lanston & Co, said a key aspect of the report was the rise in supplier delivery times index to 55.2 in May from 53.4 in April.

The supplier deliveries index, which measures the time it takes to fill orders, is "a number watched closely by Federal Reserve Chairman (Alan) Greenspan. Any reading above 55 is a sign of increasing strain in the goods producing sector of the ecomomy," he said. "This number does raise a red flag."

Jones also said the strong new orders index in May suggested that "we only saw a pause in the economy in the March-April period and will certainly see a rebound in output and therefore,in employment and incomes in the months ahead."
